title_en: Melting permafrost has birthed a new type of large landslide
title_zh: 永久冻土的融化催生了一种新型的大型滑坡

paragraphs.en: In 2018, a strange and enormous landslide occurred in Canada’s Northwest Territories. A slab of earth roughly equivalent in volume to seven Great Pyramids of Giza suddenly began sliding downhill, leaving behind a barren scar in the forested landscape. But what puzzled scientists was that the slide had initiated in frozen ground that had been glued in place for years.
paragraphs.zh: 2018年，加拿大西北地区发生了一场奇特而巨大的滑坡。一块体积大致相当于七座吉萨大金字塔的土体突然开始向下滑动，在森林覆盖的地貌中留下一道荒芜的疤痕。但令科学家困惑的是，这场滑坡始于多年来一直冻结稳固的冻土之中。

paragraphs.en: An analysis of the event reveals that it represents a new class of catastrophic landslides called permafrost detachment slides, researchers report in the Sept. 28 Geophysical Research Letters . The slides may be set in motion by wildfires that occurred decades earlier, destabilizing the ground and opening cracks through which water infiltrated deep underground. Over time, that water may have thawed the frozen layer from below, eventually unleashing the entire frozen layer in a catastrophic slide.
paragraphs.zh: 研究人员在9月28日的《地球物理研究快报》（Geophysical Research Letters）上报告说，对这次事件的分析表明，它代表了一类新的灾难性滑坡，称为多年冻土脱离滑坡。这类滑坡可能由数十年前发生的野火引发，野火破坏了地面的稳定，并打开了裂缝，使水渗入地下深处。随着时间的推移，这些水可能从下方融化了冻结层，最终使整个冻结层在灾难性滑坡中突然释放。

paragraphs.en: Large landslides don’t normally mobilize so much still-frozen material, and when they do begin in thawing layers they usually move slowly, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist studying permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study. But he says this new research suggests scientists need to better study what’s occurring beneath the surface in permafrost regions, because “we don’t know how [the ground] will move — it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”
paragraphs.zh: 阿拉斯加大学费尔班克斯分校研究多年冻土的地球物理学家德米特里·尼科尔斯基（Dmitry Nicolsky）没有参与这项研究。他说，大型滑坡通常不会 mobilise 这么多仍然冻结的物质，而当它们确实在融化层中开始时，通常移动缓慢。但他表示，这项新研究表明，科学家需要更好地研究多年冻土地区地表以下正在发生的情况，因为“我们不知道[地面]会如何移动——它可能缓慢移动，也可能灾难性地移动。”

paragraphs.en: The inspiration for the research manifested in 2019, when permafrost geologist Joseph Young, based at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, at the time, was helicoptering to a field site in the Northwest Territories to assist a colleague’s research. In some of the valleys out there, the slopes were “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” says Young, who is now at an engineering firm in Edmonton. That was surprising because they were in an area where the permafrost — ground that has been frozen for at least two consecutive years — shouldn’t have been thawing much.
paragraphs.zh: 这项研究的灵感出现在2019年，当时多年冻土地质学家约瑟夫·扬（Joseph Young）——当时任职于加拿大埃德蒙顿的阿尔伯塔大学——正乘直升机前往西北地区的一个野外地点，协助一位同事的研究。扬说，在那里的一些山谷中，山坡“到处都在崩塌，滑坡随处可见”。这令人惊讶，因为他们所在的地区，多年冻土——至少连续两年冻结的地面——本不应融化太多。扬现在在埃德蒙顿的一家工程公司工作。

paragraphs.en: Once on the ground, more puzzling details emerged. “Traditionally with permafrost, it melts from the top down, and that releases this slurry of muddy material,” Young says. But at some of the landslide sites, large blocks of still-frozen ground seemed to have been moved hundreds of meters, he says.
paragraphs.zh: 到达地面后，更多令人困惑的细节浮现出来。扬说：“传统上，多年冻土是从上往下融化的，并释放出这种泥浆状物质。”但他说，在一些滑坡地点，大块仍然冻结的地面似乎被移动了数百米。

paragraphs.en: Young and his colleagues studied two of the largest slides in the region that had moved big chunks of permafrost. These were the 2018 slide, which mobilized 18 million cubic meters of earth and dammed the Redstone River, and another event in 2017 that moved 4.5 million cubic meters of material.
paragraphs.zh: 扬和他的同事研究了该地区两起最大的滑坡，这两起滑坡移动了大块多年冻土。其中一起是2018年的滑坡，移动了1800万立方米的土体，并堵塞了红石河（Redstone River）；另一起是2017年的事件，移动了450万立方米的物质。

paragraphs.en: Field observations revealed that both events had initiated along flat sliding surfaces roughly 20 meters underground, where the permafrost layer’s base was identified. Meanwhile, satellite observations showed that the ground at both sites had been gradually moving meters each year for decades.
paragraphs.zh: 现场观察显示，这两起事件都始于地下约20米处的平坦滑动面，那里被确定为多年冻土层的底部。与此同时，卫星观测显示，两处地点的地面数十年来一直以每年数米的速度逐渐移动。

paragraphs.en: Young and his colleagues hypothesized that climate warming and wildfire had somehow played a role in causing the slides. They set up instruments nearby that tracked ground temperature from 2020 to 2022, focusing on spots either with undisturbed forest or where wildfire had burned about 25 years earlier.
paragraphs.zh: 扬和他的同事假设，气候变暖和野火以某种方式在引发这些滑坡中发挥了作用。他们在附近设置了仪器，从2020年到2022年跟踪地面温度，重点关注未受干扰的森林地点或大约25年前野火烧过的地点。
